backlog.title: From Raw Documents to AI-Ready Data — Leo Platzer & Jeff Koss
backlog.author: AI Engineer
backlog.raw_text:
A chatbot pilot on 40 hand-picked files works great. Point it at 80,000 SharePoint documents and it falls apart.

Jeff Koss and Leo Platzer, co-founder and former CTO of Deasy Labs (acquired by Collibra), walk through taking an unstructured-data AI project from stalled POC to production. Using a manufacturer building a legal-ops chatbot over 80,000 SharePoint files, they demo AI-assisted taxonomies and metadata tagging with evidence and confidence scores, sensitive-data detection, and quality checks for duplicates, conflicts and freshness. Data slices refresh on a schedule. Leo then shows why this matters: when 30% of a corpus is stale or duplicated, up to 80% of an agent's retrieved context can be useless, and cleaning it roughly doubled recall in multi-hop RAG evals. He finishes by generating a context file for coding agents with the SDK.

In this talk:
• Why document data quality means duplicates, conflicts and freshness
• AI-assisted taxonomies and metadata tagging with evidence and confidence
• Finding and filtering sensitive data before it reaches a chatbot
• How stale, duplicated data crowds out good context, and what cleaning it does to recall

backlog.title: The Transcript Looked Fine. The Call Wasn't. — Debugging Voice Agents, Arize
backlog.author: AI Engineer
backlog.raw_text:
The transcript says the agent corrected itself. The audio says it refunded the wrong order.

Fuad Ali, senior product manager at Arize AI, shows why voice agents are one of the hardest categories to debug: latency, turn-taking and transcription errors are invisible in a text log. Using a refund call that looks fine in the transcript but had 2.4 seconds of dead air, an interruption and a refund on the wrong order, he shows what you need instead. That means audio, transcript and trace in one session view, OpenInference semantic conventions for real-time audio across providers, and evals that run on the audio itself. He closes with the observe, evaluate, improve loop and agent experiments that test fixes against failed traces.

In this talk:
• Voice failure modes text logs miss: latency, barge-in, mishearing and tone
• Tracing real-time audio with open-source OpenInference conventions
• Audio-native evals for sentiment, latency, interruptions and task success
• Toward self-healing voice agents: monitors, investigation agents and replayed fixes

backlog.title: Research to Reality with Google DeepMind — Paige Bailey, Google DeepMind
backlog.author: AI Engineer
backlog.raw_text:
A model running entirely in the browser produces an emoji table ranking the Harry Potter books, and Paige Bailey immediately questions its taste. The response arrives almost instantly, without an API call or data leaving the machine. Bailey uses that demo to introduce Gemma 4, Google DeepMind's open model family, and show what local inference looks like in practice. She describes Apache 2 licensing, models ranging from two billion to 31 billion parameters, and the ability to download, adapt, and finetune them for a company's own projects. The opening also connects DeepMind's research mission to AlphaFold, medical models, robotics, and AI for science, before outlining computer use and managed agents that execute tasks in a Linux sandbox.

The same local approach extends to phones through Google AI Edge Gallery. Bailey walks through image descriptions, audio transcription, function calling, and a collection of skills for games, haikus, weather queries, and calendar events. Android and iOS devices can run downloaded models, while supported hardware accelerators handle inference instead of relying on the CPU. She then compares model size with deployment requirements: smaller GPU footprints, a single commodity GPU rather than distributed inference, laptop models, and a mobile option. Quantized checkpoints explain the speed of the browser demo, with the two billion parameter version taking less than a gigabyte. The practical thread is choosing a model that fits the device and keeping the work local.

backlog.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 2) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
backlog.author: AI Engineer
backlog.raw_text:
A request for facial recognition becomes a job statement about getting attendees into a workshop without missing the first 20 minutes. Kent C. Dodds uses that audience suggestion to separate a requested feature from the progress a user actually needs. Asking why exposes alternatives such as parallel queues or badges, rather than immediately committing to a database of faces. He breaks the job into functional, social, and emotional dimensions, showing how each changes engineering decisions. A system can move people through a door faster while making them uncomfortable about how their information is used. Success also includes whether customers keep using the product, rather than simply paying for it once.

The second exercise shifts to a food delivery app and uses the Kano model to sort competing requests. Reliable order confirmations are basic needs. Delivery estimates offer a measurable performance gradient. Discounts and group ordering can delight users, while GPS tracking illustrates how an unexpected extra becomes something customers assume will exist. Dodds connects those categories to architectural effort: make foundations reliable, measure performance, and keep experiments reversible until their value is clearer. Features that nobody cares about create maintenance work; features users actively dislike deserve pushback. Audience questions cover validating ideas before metrics exist, handling an unusually demanding customer, and understanding architecture during incidents. The closing argument ties technical expertise to product judgment: faster implementation matters when engineers understand which problems deserve solving.

backlog.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 1) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
backlog.author: AI Engineer
backlog.raw_text:
The line of attendees waiting outside becomes the workshop's live product idea: an app called Just Get In the Workshop. Kent C. Dodds uses that immediate frustration to practice deciding whether a problem deserves a software solution. Before the exercise, he explains why faster implementation changes the value of an engineer's work. Agents can help hit more targets, but choosing the useful target still requires judgment. Product engineers connect customer needs to data models, workflows, constraints, observability, and the smallest useful slice of a system. Dodds draws on conversations with other builders to show how understanding users changes architectural choices, while accepting a ticket without that context can produce technically polished work that misses the point.

The room then applies The Mom Test to its conference entry idea. Questions about whether somebody would use an app invite compliments and speculation. Questions about the last time the problem happened, what the person did instead, and what the workaround cost reveal behavior. Dodds connects that evidence to how much engineering effort a feature deserves. An experiment needs a different investment from a capability essential to the business. Early prototypes and watching people use them keep the feedback loop open after the initial idea has been validated. Audience questions explore hiring for product judgment, collaboration with product managers, and engineering responsibilities as teams grow. The first part establishes the discovery habits and technical ownership that guide the next stages of the workshop.
